item.title: Half-Click Attacks: How Online Ads Now Deliver iPhone Exploits
item.description:
DarkSword malware hit iPhones via Instagram ads from ad-track[.]live and hijacked analytics domain ecomtrack[.]io, requiring no user tap. On-device EDR must capture indicators within 2 hours before they age off.

item.title: The Supply-Chain Risk Hiding in Your MCP Servers
item.description:
MCP servers on admin workstations silently swap out dependencies between sessions, giving supply-chain attackers a path to management-plane credentials without touching the pinned release version.
Key findings:
- One community MCP server pinned to a specific Git release tag ran with 15 different dependency sets over five weeks, with 23 of its 69 packages changing versions underneath a release that looked frozen. The one-step launcher uvx resolved the full dependency tree fresh from PyPI on each rebuild, not from the project's hash-pinned lock file. A security vendor's official MCP server declared its direct dependencies with no upper version limit at all. Of 35 MCP servers reviewed from two vendor catalogs and an internal lab, 23 had a recommended install that resolved dependencies fresh from a public registry.
- The credential exposure is the core risk. MCP servers load every dependency into the same process, so code in any of roughly 70 packages runs with whatever tokens the server holds. The administrator's workstation in this case had MCP servers making more than 1,600 connections a week to 11 management systems including a firewall, SIEM, and sensor management. Malicious packages in documented real-world cases executed on import, before any server code called them.
- npm-based proxy setups carry the same risk. Several vendors' official setup instructions start the MCP auth proxy with npx at "latest" (npx proxy@latest url), pulling the newest version on every launch. One vendor's setup also disabled TLS certificate checking for the whole proxy process. A critical command-injection flaw in a widely used MCP proxy received a CVSS score of 9.6 (JFrog research, 2025): following "latest" delivered the fix quickly but would deliver a hijacked release just as fast.
- The detection path runs three layers deep. DNS logs (lookups to github[.]com, pypi[.]org, files.pythonhosted[.]org, registry.npmjs[.]org) surface candidate hosts. Zeek SSL logs fill gaps where DNS answers were cached or resolved inside containers, using the server name from the TLS handshake. EDR process network events then attribute connections to the specific launcher process and its parent (the AI coding assistant), and counting unique cache folder names in process command lines gives a rebuild count. In this investigation the administrator's workstation was the only host pulling from PyPI, 136 connections in one week, all tied to AI assistant sessions rather than any service schedule.
- The fix is a frozen install, not just a pinned release. Build the environment once from the lock file with hash checking enforced, install the server itself without re-resolving dependencies, configure the assistant to launch the installed binary directly rather than through uvx or npx, and disable startup update checks. After freezing five servers this way, the Corelight TLS logs and EDR process network events showed zero connections to GitHub or PyPI after the one-time install. The report notes that quiet network logs alone do not confirm the fix: a cached unfrozen install is also quiet between rebuilds, so the network comparison must be paired with a version check of what is actually installed on disk.
Hunt tip: query your DNS and SSL logs for the past 7 days for internal hosts contacting codeload.github[.]com, raw.githubusercontent[.]com, objects.githubusercontent[.]com, pypi[.]org, files.pythonhosted[.]org, and registry.npmjs[.]org. Developer machines are expected noise. Flag everything else, especially servers, jump hosts, and admin workstations where the process making those connections holds credentials. For each flagged host, follow the EDR process lineage and check whether the installed package versions on disk match what was there last week. The report includes a full natural-language hunt prompt you can run against Corelight DNS and SSL data directly.

item.title: Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments
item.description:
Compromised Qubole IAM credentials gave a threat actor trusted access to tens of companies' AWS environments, exfiltrating millions of files and hundreds of secrets across a 12-day campaign in October.
Key findings:
- The attacker compromised two Qubole IAM users and then abused cross-account trust relationships by calling the AWS STS AssumeRole API to step into dormant IAM roles inside customer environments. Those roles had been configured to trust Qubole's AWS account, so the assumption succeeded without triggering obvious authentication alerts. The attack window ran October 14 through 26.
- Once inside each environment, the sequence was methodical and consistent: assume the role, call ListBuckets to map accessible storage, call ListObjects and HeadObject to enumerate and inspect contents, then call GetObject to bulk-download. The attacker also retrieved secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, and Lambda environment variables, then used TruffleHog to validate harvested AWS keys, Microsoft Entra ID client secrets, and Okta credentials. That is a full credential-harvesting pass across the cloud control plane in a single access chain.
- The pace was aggressive. Sentra reported the attacker collected 100 passwords and keys in seven minutes. One customer alone lost millions of files. Tens of companies were affected in total. The approach was opportunistic: everything the assumed role could reach was downloaded, not a targeted subset.
- The core forensic signal lives in AWS CloudTrail. Reviewers should look for AssumeRole events originating from Qubole's AWS account, especially on roles that had not been recently used, followed by ListBuckets, ListObjects, HeadObject, and GetObject API calls in rapid succession. GetSecretValue calls against Secrets Manager and GetParameters against SSM Parameter Store in the same session window are further confirmation. The attacker's pattern is high-volume, wide-scope API activity immediately after a cross-account role assumption.
- How Qubole's own IAM users were initially compromised is not stated in the report, and Qubole had not made a public statement as of publication. The downstream impact, however, is a textbook illustration of third-party cloud trust chain risk: a single supplier compromise became a master key to dozens of customer environments.
Practitioner takeaway: Review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, filtering on AssumeRole where the principal account is Qubole's, then chain those session tokens forward to find every subsequent API call. Rotate any credentials that may have been exposed, revoke active role sessions, and strip or restrict any Qubole-associated roles still in your environment. Unused cross-account roles with broad S3 or Secrets Manager permissions are the attack surface here, not a vulnerability, so removal or scope reduction is the lasting fix.

item.title: Beyond ValleyRAT: inside a China-nexus Silver Fox operation
item.description:
Chinese-nexus Silver Fox spreads ValleyRAT via tax-lure packages, DLL side-loading, and a shared registrar account, in an operation running August to October 2026 across 25 loader builds and five C2 servers.
Key findings:
- The HDP loader kit powers all 44 builds VMRay Labs analysed. Delivery follows a consistent chain: a genuine signed program (renamed as a tax document, e.g. INT-Number.20260820113657.EXE or CERT-In5605112305.EXE) is dropped inside a disk image (VHDX, ISO, or VHD) inside a ZIP, side-loads an unsigned DLL loader (typically hdp.dll), which then pulls the ValleyRAT core from one of five C2 servers: taku788[.]club, fuoe333[.]club, moik77a[.]club, usdt888[.]club, and 192.252.183[.]157. The core is stored fileless in the registry under HKCU\Console\0 (registry value name 389126097FFFEF316D35ACD0610E5F31 across all six runs where a C2 answered), and persistence arrives via a scheduled task. August builds also embed two kernel drivers.
- Each build carries its own RC4-encrypted configuration. The group ID, a 19-character string stored in clear text at the start of the config, is the RC4 key written backwards. This means any analyst holding an unpacked build can decrypt its configuration and C2 settings offline without infrastructure access. Captured C2 traffic also decrypts: each session key comes from a token in message headers. Three of the four C2 domains (taku788[.]club, fuoe333[.]club, moik77a[.]club) share registrant organisation KANGYINGJIE and the hashed value ab376f4f34801a68 at Chinese 🇨🇳 registrar 22net.
- Attribution to Silver Fox rests on two independent evidence types. First, operator choices not imposed by the public ValleyRAT builder: 27 of 33 package timestamps fall in UTC+8 weekday office hours (10:00 to 17:00), signed programs come from Chinese 🇨🇳 companies (Hithink RoyalFlush, Tencent, Guangzhou Ningjinghai, Hangzhou Fencha), and registrant names at 22net are romanised Chinese 🇨🇳. Second, Gname account 574849-1923 registered two domains in Sekoia's and JUMPSEC's Silver Fox reporting, registered Indian 🇮🇳 tax lure pages, and ties to the delivery host kaiwyrey[.]eu[.]cc through a shared IP (103.23.172[.]117 on 2026-06-30) and a lure page link (kcsueaw[.]xin to the delivery host on 2026-07-31). VMRay assesses the operation very likely belongs to Silver Fox, with moderate confidence.
- Twelve builds carry the U.S. 🇺🇸 Department of Homeland Security seal as their main icon. This is the icon of the Spanish-language Visual Studio starter program the kit uses as a cover application. The loader never loads or displays it; VMRay run logs recorded no icon resource lookups across nine runs of these builds. The seal is almost certainly an artifact of the cover application template, not a lure element.
- The delivery host kaiwyrey[.]eu[.]cc served loaders for three C2 servers in sequence: auk218[.]club (outside the operation, 2026-08-03 to 08-13), then 192.252.183[.]157 (the operation's IP, 08-17 to 08-31), then fddlbh2[.]club (09-02 to 09-06). fddlbh2[.]club was registered roughly 13.5 hours after B4's package was last recorded on the delivery host, and was pointed to 192.252.183[.]157 within about 15 hours of registration.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt HKCU\Console\0 for the registry value 389126097FFFEF316D35ACD0610E5F31 (packed ValleyRAT core). Look for mutexes beginning with a pipe character followed by a 19-character group ID. Flag unsigned DLLs sitting beside renamed signed executables loaded from mounted disk images. Flag delivery archives whose names end in a 14-digit timestamp and 12 hex characters (e.g. 20260902110114-0AFC3F174BAD[.]zip): those hex characters are the start of the build's RC4 config key. Rebuild any host carrying the registry value or the scheduled task; the core grants full remote control and August builds drop kernel drivers. The full 1,391-indicator set (network, file, config, and host artifacts), plus a machine-readable CSV and the technical annex with offline decryption methods, are in the report.

item.title: Three China-Nexus Espionage Campaigns Linked Through Sparrow Malware Ecosystem
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage quartermaster CopperDragon linked to three active clusters hitting telecoms, governments, and critical infrastructure across Latin America, Asia, and Europe through a shared Sparrow malware ecosystem.
Key findings:
- CopperDragon operates as a digital quartermaster supplying tools to multiple China-nexus actors including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, and Tropic Trooper. Three clusters, SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire, initially appeared independent but share code and infrastructure under the Sparrow framework. FamousSparrow carries assessed overlap with Salt Typhoon, though the exact relationship is unresolved.
- SilentDelivery (early 2026) runs watering hole attacks against government, shipping, IT, and research sites in Czech 🇨🇿 Republic, Germany 🇩🇪, France 🇫🇷, Taiwan 🇹🇼, and others, injecting jsjiami-obfuscated JavaScript that fingerprints visitors by IP and geolocation before serving a fake Chrome SSL warning and dropping a trojanized MSI disguised as a "Certificate Fix" utility. The payload is SquadC (also called SquawkDoor), a C/C++ Windows backdoor that persists via a Registry Run key masquerading as a Windows update assistant. A secondary delivery chain targets Indonesian 🇮🇩 organizations via phishing LNK files that abuse the legitimate ftp.exe binary to execute a batch script and sideload SquadC.
- OceanGate (2025-2026) enters through internet-facing Linux servers, deploying AnnobinDoor, a Go-based backdoor with SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, and reverse shell capability, and SparrowShell, a modular Linux backdoor sharing code with SparrowDoor and with Mélofée (the Reptile rootkit-based implant documented in 2023), raising the possibility CopperDragon also authored Mélofée. After credential harvesting across multiple Linux accounts, the actor pivots to Windows via RDP password-spraying until it authenticates as an administrator, then deploys CopperAdu, CopperList, CopperLogger (Raw Input keylogger with clipboard and active window monitoring), and CopperLsa for NTLM and Kerberos credential theft. SparrowDoor is then weaponized with WinDivert kernel drivers, converting it to a passive backdoor that intercepts packets at kernel level, internally redirecting connections from port 443 to a high internal port such as 49628, with responses rewritten to appear to originate from the legitimate service.
- DarkWire (mid-2025) focuses on Latin American telecoms and government entities. CopperDoor, a memory-resident modular backdoor, and CopperDNS, a variant using DNS tunneling over MX queries, are delivered via CopperLoader through DLL sideloading of executables not commonly abused by other actors. The cluster deliberately avoids creating new directories, dropping tools into existing system paths to reduce footprint. Infrastructure was deliberately sourced from within victim countries to blend C2 traffic with local network patterns. CopperLsass handles LSASS dumping for credential harvesting; CopperProxy and PyProxy (a Python UDP relay) support network pivoting.
Practitioner takeaway: The cross-cluster pivot is the most actionable thread. Hunt for DLL sideloading of uncommon legitimate executables in existing system paths, ftp.exe spawning batch processes, and RDP authentication events following Linux-side credential harvesting. On Linux, look for Go-based implants and rootkit drivers consistent with Reptile. For the watering hole chain, proxy or DNS logs showing victim browsers receiving MSI files from government or shipping sector domains after a certificate-warning page are a high-fidelity signal. Check Point's report contains IOCs and technical indicators across all three clusters.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Xen Orchestra Auth Bypass Flaw to Gain Admin Access
item.description:
Critical Xen Orchestra auth bypass is under active exploitation, granting attackers full admin access and root-level takeover of XCP-ng hypervisor nodes without valid credentials.
Key details:
- The flaw (VSA-2026-062, no CVE assigned yet) lives in REST cookie parsing. Sending authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D causes the server to parse the token as an empty object {}. That object passes to the XO token provider, which treats it as an unfiltered lookup and returns the first unexpired token in the collection, authenticating the caller as that token's owner. A follow-up request to /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens then hands the attacker reusable login token IDs, all without knowing any credential.
- Once authenticated as Admin, the attacker can execute arbitrary code on managed pools and take full root control of XCP-ng nodes. The active exploitation infrastructure includes 91.211.251[.]112:8001 (flagged on VirusTotal as a RedLine Stealer C2) and the Tor endpoint ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333. Whether this was a zero-day before disclosure is not yet confirmed.
- For responders, the host-side IOCs are concrete and worth hunting now: a running VM named pivot2, VMs configured with the hvm_serial: file parameter, and four suspicious files at /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6. item.title: Russia-Linked APT Turla Turned Exchange Servers Into Their Own Control Room
item.description:
Russia-linked Turla APT deployed a previously undocumented .NET toolset called Cereal against government Exchange servers in Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 and Romania 🇷🇴, using the victim's own server as a passive C2 node with no external attacker infrastructure to find or block.
Key findings:
- ESET attributes Cereal with high confidence to Turla (aka Secret Blizzard, Snake, Uroburos, Waterbug, Venomous Bear, KRYPTON), assessed by CISA as affiliated with Center 16 of Russia's 🇷🇺 FSB. First victim was a Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 government body on 28 November 2025; Romania 🇷🇴 followed on 23 December 2025, with the Romanian 🇷🇴 deployment specifically configured to intercept emails to or from NATO and EU contacts.
- The core backdoor, CerealNeuron, is a passive implant dropped onto internet-facing Exchange servers. It carries no built-in commands and spawns no outbound connection. Instead it listens on web paths designed to blend with normal Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic. Malformed or unauthenticated requests receive a legitimate-looking Exchange error page, making the implant invisible in firewall logs. ESET was unable to identify any operator IP addresses.
- Commands are delivered as small compiled .NET assemblies carried by CerealRunner inside encrypted network requests. Observed task modules cover mailbox collection via Exchange Web Services, Active Directory enumeration, WMI queries, extraction of locally stored Windows credentials, and file operations. ESET observed enough near-identical binaries to infer Turla runs an internal build system that generates them on demand. A disk-resident variant, CerealHermit, reads encrypted command files directly from disk, giving operators a second access path on some victims.
- Email theft is handled by CerealBox, which injects into EdgeTransport.exe, the Exchange process managing mail flow, and wraps the transport agent handlers already running in memory. Because CerealBox registers no new agent, nothing anomalous appears in Exchange transport agent configuration. It filters for messages carrying .doc, .docx, or .pdf attachments matching hardcoded sender, recipient, subject, or filename criteria, then compresses, encrypts, and stages selected messages on disk for later operator collection.
- Loader tradecraft exploits a rarely used .NET feature to execute native code before the managed entry point fires, so static analysis sees a no-op. Turla placed the first loader in the Windows management folder as ncobjapi.dll and in the .NET native image cache as Microsoft[.]Exchange[.]Search.Mdb[.]ni.dll, causing trusted Exchange processes to load the implant on their behalf.
Takeaway for responders: a clean Exchange transport agent list does not rule out CerealBox. Inspect the running memory of EdgeTransport.exe for injected .NET code wrapping existing agent handlers. Hunt for unexpected DLLs in the Windows management folder and unfamiliar .ni.dll files in the .NET native image cache. Review IIS logs for anomalous request patterns against Autodiscover, ActiveSync, and OWA paths, especially low-volume encrypted POST requests that return Exchange-standard error codes. Prioritize internet-facing Exchange servers at government, diplomatic, and defense-adjacent organizations in former Soviet republics and European NATO members. The ESET report is the source for deeper component details.

item.title: Php2shell: A Network Edge Risk Playbook
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS 9.2) are actively exploited PHP RCE flaws hitting network appliance management interfaces. CISA KEV-listed, with confirmed PAN-OS exploitation and 25 servers rooted including US 🇺🇸 government systems.
Key findings:
- Both CVEs were fixed by the PHP project on October 21, 2026, but appliance owners cannot patch PHP themselves. Each vendor compiled PHP into firmware, so every vendor must ship its own fixed build. Of 55 vendors tracked, only 15 have fully fixed every affected product line. Netgear has at least one supported product with no fix and no date. Seven vendors (A10 Networks, Array Networks, Imperva, Lenovo, NVIDIA networking, Radware, TP-Link) have issued no public statement at all. Treat silence as unknown, not safe.
- Palo Alto Networks is the only vendor confirming active exploitation. PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet were targeted before October 26, when CISA added both CVEs to KEV. Dream Research documented post-exploitation artifacts on rooted devices: a 103-byte PHP web shell at /unauth/php/change_password.php (PAN-OS ships a legitimate file under that name, so check size and contents), tunnel scripts under /usr/local/lib/.panops/ started by a systemd service and an rc.local hook, /etc/pam.d/su overwritten to use pam_permit.so (allowing local privilege escalation without a password), a reverse SSH tunnel across eight ports, and a SAML configuration with validate-idp-certificate set to no. The attacker also decrypted an LDAP service account credential from the rooted firewall.
- For IR triage on PAN-OS: any management interface or GlobalProtect portal reachable from untrusted networks after October 17 should be treated as a candidate for compromise review. Unit 42's hunt query targets Threat ID 543004 in next-generation firewall threat logs, but only where Threat Prevention content was installed and logging. The SAML configuration flag and roughly 900 MB of multipart POST traffic with oversized filenames are checkable in firewall config and network or proxy logs without appliance filesystem access. File-system indicators require working with Palo Alto support, as PAN-OS does not expose the filesystem through normal admin interfaces.
- Several product lines will never receive a fix. NetScaler ADC and Gateway 13.0 (Eclypsium's lab confirmed PHP 7.3.7 on the management interface), Check Point firewalls R80 through R81 and Spark R77.20.x and R80.20.x (all end of support), Ivanti Endpoint Security (reaching end of life December 31, 2026), Siemens Energy Engage V2.0SP9 (no fix planned), and legacy PHP packages on ASUSTOR ADM 3.5 and 4.0 have no fix path. For these, management interface isolation to trusted administrator hosts is the only interim control until replacement is funded and scheduled.
- F5 backported both fixes, so fixed BIG-IP builds (21.1.0.4, 17.5.1.11, 17.1.3.7) still report PHP 5.4.45 to scanners. Do not use the PHP version string or internet-wide scan counts to determine patch state. Use the appliance version and the vendor advisory (K000163821 for F5) to confirm fix status. Censys counts over 4 million PHP-reporting hosts but cannot distinguish patched appliances from vulnerable ones.
Takeaway: If you have PAN-OS with an internet-facing management interface or GlobalProtect portal that was unpatched after October 17, begin compromise review now. Patching does not evict an attacker already present, and it does not remove the web shell, tunnel scripts, or altered PAM configuration Dream Research documented. Rotate every credential stored on any firewall that shows those indicators, and work device recovery with Palo Alto support. For every other appliance in your environment, map which ones have PHP-backed management interfaces, confirm their fix status against the vendor advisory (not the PHP version string), and restrict management access to trusted hosts immediately. IOCs and post-exploitation indicators are detailed in the Dream Research write-up and the Eclypsium report.

item.title: ARTEX: Attackers apply agentic AI
item.description:
Agentic AI is now a live threat actor tool. ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent pentest framework, was used in real intrusions weeks after its July 2026 release, including by Chinese 🇨🇳 state-aligned Storm-0940.
Key details:
- ARTEX is written in Go, supports multiple LLM providers, and has been run against cloud APIs using stolen credentials. In the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise in mid-October 2026, Microsoft attributes the intrusion to Storm-0940. Microsoft's report states the group was using ARTEX "as early as September 2026," and a separate incident the same month targeted South Korean 🇰🇷 financial organizations. The framework uses planning agents to map targets and select next steps, worker agents to invoke tooling, and runs multiple breach paths in parallel, logging discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph as it goes.
- The attack chain relies on pre-obtained access, stolen application credentials, consented third-party apps, or valid accounts, fed into ARTEX to drive autonomous targeting of cloud APIs and services including Microsoft Graph. Observed behaviors include webshell deployment, SQL Server command execution, credential theft, and lateral movement. What sets this apart from traditional tooling is scale: Sophos observed hundreds of protection events across a small number of customers, with rapid command sequences, small repeated variants, and structured output markers like MARKER123 and ARTX123 written to temp files.
- Host-side artifacts are distinctive. Hunt for temporary files named i<intentID>[variant]_<purpose>.<ext>, for example i12345_b2.ps1, and for files or paths beginning with artx, particularly under C:\Windows\Temp. Structured markers (MARKER123, ARTX123) in command output combined with burst command patterns and repeated variants are strong behavioral signals of agent-driven execution.
- In cloud environments, look for service principal credentials added or roles assigned by an application, and application sign-ins carrying a scripted user agent. Sophos recommends auditing Microsoft Entra ID service principals and enterprise applications, reviewing every credential addition and role assignment since September 2026. Alert on scripted user agent sign-ins and abnormal authentication failure rates.
- A backdoored copy of the ARTEX Docker image is detected as Troj/Bckdr-SDA. The original project has been taken offline by its developer, so any copy sourced from an unofficial mirror or clone should be treated as untrusted. Sophos has released Sophos Firewall and Endpoint IPS signatures covering network-observable ARTEX behaviors; the report names the specific rule IDs covering initial access, credential theft, lateral movement, webshell activity, and Active Adversary Protection disruption rules.
Practitioner takeaway: start your threat hunt from September 2026. On hosts, grep process command lines and temp directories for artx paths and MARKER123/ARTX123 markers. In Entra ID, pull the audit log for credential additions and role assignments to service principals made by applications, not by humans, since that date. Automate containment of compromised service principals via playbook: when a principal reaches privileged access quickly, disable and revoke before an analyst reviews, not after.

item.title: Critical Xen Orchestra auth bypass flaw exploited to hijack VM servers
item.description:
Critical auth bypass VSA-2026-062 in Xen Orchestra is actively exploited, letting unauthenticated attackers claim admin sessions and take full root control of XCP-ng virtualization hosts.
Key findings:
- The flaw lives in how Xen Orchestra processes REST API authentication cookies. Sending the cookie authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D (an empty JSON object) tricks the platform into fetching an existing token and logging the attacker in as that token's owner, with no credentials required. Once in, the attacker hits /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens to harvest reusable login token IDs for persistent access. No CVE or CVSS score has been assigned yet; it is tracked as VSA-2026-062.
- The confirmed post-auth impact is severe: arbitrary code execution on managed pools and full root takeover of XCP-ng nodes. Vates confirmed active exploitation in the wild and published IOCs tied to a known campaign, noting other actors may use different infrastructure.
- Campaign IOCs from the advisory include the attacker IP 91.211.251[.]112:8001 and the Tor hidden service ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333, a VM named pivot2, virtual machines configured with hvm_serial: file, and the files /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6.
- Vates explicitly warns that exploitation leaves no log entries for the crafted cookie itself: the malicious authentication request does not appear in XCP-ng or Xen Orchestra logs. Detection requires HTTP-level traffic monitoring of the management interface, not log review alone.
Responder takeaway: on any exposed Xen Orchestra instance, run the three hunt commands Vates published. "xe vm-list params=name-label,platform | grep -B1 'hvm_serial: file'" catches VMs wired for serial-file output. "zgrep -- '-serial file:' /var/log/xensource.log*" looks for the same pattern in rotated Xen logs. "ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /.ustar* /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar*" surfaces the known implant files. If compromised, rotate all passwords and secrets tied to the virtualization environment. Patch to xo-server 5.211.2 or 5.213.1 (shipped in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0). Until patching is possible, isolate the management interface to a dedicated management network.

item.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
item.description:
Zero-day exploit chain in AhsayCBS drops a host-locked Python backdoor, five JSP web shell families, dual XMRig miners, and tunneling tools, with credential theft from a connected Veeam server hinting at deliberate backup infrastructure targeting.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 were chained as zero-days to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on AhsayCBS. Ahsay Backup released patches in mid-October 2026. The actor moved fast initially with a smash-and-grab miner drop, then slowed down and built deep persistence, a pattern that suggests the operator reused an opportunistic entry point for a more deliberate intrusion.
- Five JSP web shell families were planted across the server. AhsayCBS.jsp is the most notable: it hides encrypted payloads inside PNG pixel data and executes them from memory, disguising itself as an internal image preview service. The status_ and st_ variants name themselves with six random letters (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), execute commands, recursively delete paths on demand, and self-delete. nsmind.jsp exposes exec, cd, upload, and download parameters. Because AhsayCBS.jsp uses only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, it compiles on any servlet container from JDK 6 onward, maximising portability.
- The Python implant (main[.]py) is built to resist sandbox analysis. It computes the SHA-256 hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file of the same name in its own directory before proceeding. Only if that marker exists does it load an embedded x64 DLL into memory and beacon to creepexplosiondarknight[.]com. No MachineGuid match means no execution, so dynamic analysis on a generic sandbox image produces nothing. Microsoft Defender exclusions were configured to reduce on-host visibility.
- Two separate XMRig miners ran simultaneously using different wallets and mining pools. One masqueraded as Microsoft Edge. The second, kvm-agent.exe, was kept alive by a SYSTEM-level scheduled task set to restart every minute. GOST, Chisel, AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop were all deployed for tunneling and persistent remote access.
- On a Veeam server in the same environment, a PowerShell script launched remotely through WMI queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database and decrypted stored credentials using DPAPI. The Huntress report frames this as intentional: backup software holds hypervisor, repository, and domain account credentials, and the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query points to an operator who targeted backup infrastructure on purpose.

Zero-day exploit chain in AhsayCBS drops a host-locked Python backdoor, five JSP web shell families, dual XMRig miners, and tunneling tools, with credential theft from a connected Veeam server hinting at deliberate backup infrastructure targeting.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 were chained as zero-days to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on AhsayCBS. Ahsay Backup released patches in mid-October 2026. The actor moved fast initially with a smash-and-grab miner drop, then slowed down and built deep persistence, a pattern that suggests the operator reused an opportunistic entry point for a more deliberate intrusion.

- Five JSP web shell families were planted across the server. AhsayCBS.jsp is the most notable: it hides encrypted payloads inside PNG pixel data and executes them from memory, disguising itself as an internal image preview service. The status_ and st_ variants name themselves with six random letters (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), execute commands, recursively delete paths on demand, and self-delete. nsmind.jsp exposes exec, cd, upload, and download parameters. Because AhsayCBS.jsp uses only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, it compiles on any servlet container from JDK 6 onward, maximising portability.

- The Python implant (main[.]py) is built to resist sandbox analysis. It computes the SHA-256 hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file of the same name in its own directory before proceeding. Only if that marker exists does it load an embedded x64 DLL into memory and beacon to creepexplosiondarknight[.]com. No MachineGuid match means no execution, so dynamic analysis on a generic sandbox image produces nothing. Microsoft Defender exclusions were configured to reduce on-host visibility.

- Two separate XMRig miners ran simultaneously using different wallets and mining pools. One masqueraded as Microsoft Edge. The second, kvm-agent.exe, was kept alive by a SYSTEM-level scheduled task set to restart every minute. GOST, Chisel, AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop were all deployed for tunneling and persistent remote access.

- On a Veeam server in the same environment, a PowerShell script launched remotely through WMI queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database and decrypted stored credentials using DPAPI. item.title: GhostFrame: A new ESXi Implant Linked to Settra Ransomware
item.description:
GhostFrame, a previously undocumented ESXi post-exploitation framework, gives TAG-218 root-to-hypervisor control over VMware environments and has been directly linked to Settra ransomware intrusions targeting US 🇺🇸 and European organizations.
Key findings:
- TAG-218 used GhostFrame alongside MeshCentral RMM after gaining initial access through VPN appliances, predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices, between late August and October 2026. Activity aligns with CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass in Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that lets attackers establish VPN sessions without valid credentials or MFA. Four targeted organizations subsequently appeared on the Settra ransomware leak site. On October 12, 2026, a victim Fortinet VPN appliance was observed beaconing to both GhostFrame and MeshCentral simultaneously, placing GhostFrame squarely in the intrusion chain.
- The implant, named vmhostd-core, persists by copying itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and modifying /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh to execute at boot. Every five seconds the boot script re-disables the ESXi firewall and sets execInstalledOnly to 0, so simply re-enabling those controls without removing the persistence mechanism accomplishes nothing. The implant then calls /sbin/auto-backup.sh to survive reboots and masquerades as vmhostd, mimicking VMware's legitimate vmware-hostd daemon at the process level.
- C2 communication is behaviorally distinctive: the implant fires near-simultaneous TCP SYN packets to the same destination IP across six ports, 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443, and 9443, using whichever connects first and dropping the rest. That six-way SYN burst from an ESXi host to a single external IP is a high-fidelity network detection opportunity. Once connected, the implant operates as an in-memory shellcode loader, receiving and executing payloads without writing them to disk.
- From the hypervisor layer GhostFrame reaches every hosted VM without touching them individually. The sdkmon credential interceptor modifies ESXi service configuration to capture authentication traffic from subsequent logins. VMkatz, an integrated open-source tool, extracts NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets, and NTDS.dit data via VM memory snapshots or virtual disk images. A SOCKS5 proxy component named gfsox routes traffic through the hypervisor into otherwise unreachable internal segments.
Takeaway: Hunt your ESXi hosts now. Check /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh for added lines calling vmhostd-core or disabling the firewall and execInstalledOnly. Look for a process named vmhostd spawned from an unusual parent path, especially /opt/vmhostd-core. On the network side, write a detection for six near-simultaneous TCP SYN packets from a single ESXi host to the same external IP across the port set above, that pattern is framework-level behavior that survives C2 rotation. IOCs are in the full Insikt Group report.

item.title: Not All That Glitters Is Gold: Tracking CopperDragon’s Sparrow Framework Around the Globe
item.description:
CopperDragon, a likely Chinese 🇨🇳 digital quartermaster, is supplying the cross-platform Sparrow malware framework to multiple China-nexus APTs across three distinct global clusters hitting telcos, governments, and military targets in Latin America, Asia, and Europe.
Key findings:
- CopperDragon connects FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, and UAT-9244 through shared tooling and infrastructure. The Sparrow framework now spans Windows and Linux with a toolkit that includes SparrowDoor, SparrowShell, SquadC, CopperDoor, CopperDNS, CopperLoader, CopperLsa, CopperLogger, CopperAdu, CopperList, CopperLsass, AnnobinDoor, and Trojanized SSH components. SparrowShell shares code, RC4 keys, and rootkit design with the Melofee backdoor, and the report assesses CopperDragon supplies Melofee variants as well. The full IOC table is in the report.
- SilentDelivery uses watering-hole attacks on government, shipping, and IT sector websites, injecting jsjiami-obfuscated JavaScript that fingerprints visitors via /image-check?t=datetime requests, then serves a fake Chrome SSL error page pushing a Trojanized MSI named CertFixer.msi that delivers the SquadC backdoor. SquadC persists via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run under the key WindowsUpdateAssist, checks for running browsers (chrome.exe, msedge.exe, firefox.exe, brave.exe, edge.exe) before executing, and reports successful compromise to /register-ip on the C2. A parallel spearphishing chain abuses ftp.exe as a LOLBin via an LNK inside a RAR archive named Strategi_AS_Referensi_April2026.rar. C2 infrastructure includes microsfot[.]vip, microscoft[.]vip, aistei[.]com, 135.136.135[.]54, and 103.141.235[.]123.
- OceanGate begins with Linux server exploitation, deploys the Go-based AnnobinDoor backdoor and the modular SparrowShell with an embedded modified Reptile rootkit loaded via init_module and controlled through ioctl ID 0x0e0e0e0e. The actor then replaced legitimate SSH binaries with credential-harvesting Trojanized versions before pivoting to Windows over RDP. On Windows, CopperAdu creates a hidden local account (admin$, hardcoded password Admin@123456), sets LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy to 1, and opens SMB on TCP 445 under a firewall rule named RasiUwpApp. CopperLsa registers a malicious LSA security package inside LSASS to harvest NTLM and Kerberos credentials. SparrowDoor variants abuse WinDivert drivers to operate as a passive backdoor, intercepting packets destined for port 443 and silently rewriting them to an internal high port such as 49628, with connections gated on the magic value 0x11223344.
- DarkWire targets Latin American telecom operators and government entities using CopperLoader, a reflective DLL sideloading shellcode loader that decrypts next-stage payloads from .dat files using RC4. It delivers CopperDoor (also known as SparroWocky, analyzed by ESET), which uses call stack spoofing and gadget-based execution for EDR evasion, and CopperDNS, a variant tunneling C2 traffic over DNS MX queries. CopperLsass injects slave.dll into LSASS via RPC, dumps memory using comsvcs.dll, encrypts the dump with a SUB-XOR-ADD algorithm, and stages the result as 1.png for exfiltration. SoftEther VPN was renamed vmtoolsd.exe and csrss.exe for cover, and tools were placed in existing paths including C:\Windows\debug, C:\ProgramData\vmware\logs, and C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java. The domain amelicen[.]com ties DarkWire infrastructure directly to previously reported SparrowDoor C2 activity. CopperDNS nodes reuse a distinctive TLS certificate (SHA-256: ee4a8b81fe3864582efc27a77f806990e2602dcc36447ddda4b3a230a473d575) with CN=8.8.8.8 across multiple servers on high port 6532.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for WindowsUpdateAssist in Run keys and CertFixer.msi execution on endpoints in government and telco environments. On Linux hosts, check for unsigned kernel modules loaded via init_module, Trojanized SSH binaries, and iptables rules added programmatically. On Windows, look for LSASS children loading unexpected security packages, the RasiUwpApp firewall rule, and an admin$ local account. Monitor for DNS MX query bursts to low-reputation domains as a CopperDNS indicator. Full IOC tables covering hashes, domains, and IPs for all three clusters are in the Check Point Research report.

item.title: Turla’s Cereal malware turns victims’ Exchange servers into spy hubs
item.description:
Russia-linked Turla planted modular .NET spyware on Exchange servers at two government targets, one in Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 and one in Romania 🇷🇴, intercepting email mid-flight before it ever left the building, with the victim's own server acting as the attacker's command post.
Key findings:
- ESET attributes the toolset, named Cereal, to Turla (also known as Snake) with high confidence, linking it to a previously documented Turla component used alongside it and to similarities with older Turla malware. Turla is widely assessed to be part of Russia's 🇷🇺 FSB. The Kazakh 🇰🇿 victim was identified November 28, 2025, the Romanian 🇷🇴 victim December 23, 2025. In Romania 🇷🇴, the collection module was explicitly scoped to messages involving NATO and EU addresses. Activity in Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 surged January 15, 2026, the day after the Old New Year, suggesting the operators took the Russian 🇷🇺 holiday off.
- The core backdoor, CerealNeuron, listens on paths that mimic legitimate Exchange traffic such as /owa/sdds/ and /autodiscover/proxyservice/. Only requests that pass encryption and integrity checks get executed; everything else receives a valid-looking Exchange error page. Commands arrive as small, purpose-built .NET binaries covering mailbox access, Active Directory queries, LSA secret extraction, and file operations. The near-identical structure of these binaries points to an automated build framework. A second backdoor, CerealHermit, operates entirely offline, reading encrypted command files from disk as a fallback.
- The email interception component, CerealBox, does not register a new Exchange transport agent (which would appear in Exchange configuration). Instead it injects into EdgeTransport.exe at runtime and wraps the handlers of transport agents already loaded in memory, leaving no visible new agent. It filters for messages carrying .doc, .docx, or .pdf attachments that match hardcoded sender, recipient, subject, or attachment-name lists, then compresses, encrypts, and stages copies on disk for later collection. ESET states this in-process transport hooking technique has not been documented for any prior malware family.
- The Cereal loader is the only component written to disk as a recognizable .NET file, but it executes native code before the .NET runtime reaches its normal entry point, so static analysis of the .NET layer sees a program that appears to do nothing. In one deployment it masqueraded as ncobjapi.dll placed in C:\Windows\System32\wbem, loaded automatically by the WMI service. In another it posed as wbemcomn.dll. Operators also placed malicious copies into the .NET native image cache under names such as Microsoft[.]Exchange[.]Search.Mdb[.]ni.dll, causing Exchange to load the malicious file before falling back to the legitimate library.
DFIR takeaway: On any Exchange server in scope, examine C:\Windows\System32\wbem for unexpected DLLs (ncobjapi.dll and wbemcomn.dll), audit the .NET native image cache for files with Exchange-resembling names that do not match known-good hashes, and review EdgeTransport.exe memory for injected modules. The absence of a registered transport agent in Exchange configuration is not evidence of a clean system: look at what is loaded in-process. For the network side, CerealNeuron leaves no attacker-owned C2 to block since it repurposes the victim's own server, so hunting outbound indicators will not find it. Focus on the Exchange IIS logs for unusual request patterns on paths like /owa/sdds/ and /autodiscover/proxyservice/ that return errors rather than valid session activity. The report contains component details and the attack chain diagram.

item.title: Formbook Targets European Manufacturing and Technology Businesses with Localized Order Lures
item.description:
Formbook/XLoader campaign hits UK 🇬🇧 and Italian 🇮🇹 manufacturing and technology firms with localized procurement lures, using a four-stage chain of obfuscated JavaScript, AES-encrypted PowerShell, and process hollowing to steal browser credentials.
- The infection begins with a ZIP archive containing a heavily obfuscated JavaScript file, Nova narudžba 0148-712.js (SHA-256: a970e997093fcd10d108354423c8fa420a6887ed97cbf7c7dbe3551faa4d9b95), whose Croatian/Bosnian title means "New Order". The JS decodes a Base64-embedded PowerShell payload, writes a randomly named ps_[random]_[timestamp].ps1 script to C:\Temp\ (falling back to %TEMP%), establishes persistence, and launches PowerShell with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -NonInteractive. A WMI watchdog kills the process if it runs beyond 50 seconds. For responders, wscript.exe spawning hidden PowerShell writing randomized scripts to C:\Temp\ is the first pivot point.
- Stage 2 is an AES-256-CBC PowerShell loader (b0ee22dee7a8a9710992294f73069f047d31506b50dc1150ef6013fcd6225ed1) that stores the payload, key, and IV as three Base64 resources, decrypts the next stage in memory via ScriptBlock::Create(), then clears its resource map. The infection is not fully fileless: the original JS and intermediate PS1 remain on disk and are recoverable as forensic evidence.
- Stage 3 delivers GHOST.dll (SHA-256: 2974a808e24e76c1a9fecdaaecebefe27e841204bc1aa20536c32c1f0b309f47), a ConfuserEx-protected .NET injector that hollows Formbook into aspnet_compiler.exe. A watchdog named Operate-Beacon polls every five seconds and reinjects if the process dies, producing 15 aspnet_compiler.exe launches in the sandbox session. Formbook then migrates into rekeywiz.exe, launches Firefox, and drops a randomly named file in %TEMP% to collect browser databases. The same GHOST.dll previously appeared as cloked_data.exe in a separate analysis on October 9, 2026, suggesting loader reuse across builds.
- Persistence uses the naming pattern SystemUpdate_ps_* across three mechanisms: a Run key under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, an attempted Run key under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, and a startup shortcut SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk in the Windows Startup folder with the description "System Update Service". C2 runs over HTTP port 80 to www.hlushkova[.]top/ef5f/ and www.stanbicfinanceug[.]com/9wgi/ (IPs: 91.234.194[.]113, 2.58.67[.]83, 5.9.115[.]199). A Windows host sending HTTP traffic with an Android 4.1.1 User-Agent is a reliable proxy-log detection signal. The first domain changed resolved IPs during observation, so domain-based blocking is preferable to IP-only controls.
- Threat intelligence correlation shows the C:\Temp\ps_*.ps1 file path pattern appeared in 78 sandbox analyses over 90 days, linked to AgentTesla, DarkCloud, Remcos, XWorm, and Snake. The SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk persistence artifact appeared in 42 analyses and the registry value in 24, overlapping with AsyncRAT and Snake Keylogger as well. This points to a shared loader or distribution mechanism broader than this single Formbook campaign.
Hunt the execution chain: wscript.exe spawning powershell.exe with hidden parameters, writing ps_*.ps1 to C:\Temp\, followed by repeated aspnet_compiler.exe launches and rekeywiz.exe with an unexpected parent. Correlate with SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk in the Startup folder and the matching Run key values. The full IOC table, including six file hashes, two domains, two URLs, and three IPs, is in the report.

item.content:encoded:
Formbook/XLoader campaign hits UK 🇬🇧 and Italian 🇮🇹 manufacturing and technology firms with localized procurement lures, using a four-stage chain of obfuscated JavaScript, AES-encrypted PowerShell, and process hollowing to steal browser credentials.

- The infection begins with a ZIP archive containing a heavily obfuscated JavaScript file, Nova narudžba 0148-712.js (SHA-256: a970e997093fcd10d108354423c8fa420a6887ed97cbf7c7dbe3551faa4d9b95), whose Croatian/Bosnian title means "New Order". The JS decodes a Base64-embedded PowerShell payload, writes a randomly named ps_[random]_[timestamp].ps1 script to C:\Temp\ (falling back to %TEMP%), establishes persistence, and launches PowerShell with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -NonInteractive. A WMI watchdog kills the process if it runs beyond 50 seconds. For responders, wscript.exe spawning hidden PowerShell writing randomized scripts to C:\Temp\ is the first pivot point.

- Stage 2 is an AES-256-CBC PowerShell loader (b0ee22dee7a8a9710992294f73069f047d31506b50dc1150ef6013fcd6225ed1) that stores the payload, key, and IV as three Base64 resources, decrypts the next stage in memory via ScriptBlock::Create(), then clears its resource map. The infection is not fully fileless: the original JS and intermediate PS1 remain on disk and are recoverable as forensic evidence.

- Stage 3 delivers GHOST.dll (SHA-256: 2974a808e24e76c1a9fecdaaecebefe27e841204bc1aa20536c32c1f0b309f47), a ConfuserEx-protected .NET injector that hollows Formbook into aspnet_compiler.exe. A watchdog named Operate-Beacon polls every five seconds and reinjects if the process dies, producing 15 aspnet_compiler.exe launches in the sandbox session. Formbook then migrates into rekeywiz.exe, launches Firefox, and drops a randomly named file in %TEMP% to collect browser databases. The same GHOST.dll previously appeared as cloked_data.exe in a separate analysis on October 9, 2026, suggesting loader reuse across builds.

- Persistence uses the naming pattern SystemUpdate_ps_* across three mechanisms: a Run key under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, an attempted Run key under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, and a startup shortcut SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk in the Windows Startup folder with the description "System Update Service". C2 runs over HTTP port 80 to www.hlushkova[.]top/ef5f/ and www.stanbicfinanceug[.]com/9wgi/ (IPs: 91.234.194[.]113, 2.58.67[.]83, 5.9.115[.]199). A Windows host sending HTTP traffic with an Android 4.1.1 User-Agent is a reliable proxy-log detection signal. The first domain changed resolved IPs during observation, so domain-based blocking is preferable to IP-only controls.

- Threat intelligence correlation shows the C:\Temp\ps_*.ps1 file path pattern appeared in 78 sandbox analyses over 90 days, linked to AgentTesla, DarkCloud, Remcos, XWorm, and Snake. The SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk persistence artifact appeared in 42 analyses and the registry value in 24, overlapping with AsyncRAT and Snake Keylogger as well. This points to a shared loader or distribution mechanism broader than this single Formbook campaign.

Hunt the execution chain: wscript.exe spawning powershell.exe with hidden parameters, writing ps_*.ps1 to C:\Temp\, followed by repeated aspnet_compiler.exe launches and rekeywiz.exe with an unexpected parent. Correlate with SystemUpdate_ps_*.lnk in the Startup folder and the matching Run key values. The full IOC table, including six file hashes, two domains, two URLs, and three IPs, is in the report.

item.title: Dark Web Profile: CyberXero
item.description:
Russian-speaking IAB CyberXero runs dual campaigns: mass WordPress exploitation globally and curated reconnaissance against Ukrainian 🇺🇦 energy infrastructure, augmented by a swarm of 51 AI agents wired into Cobalt Strike.
Key details:
- Attribution rests on an exposed open directory containing over 90,000 files from an active Linux workstation, including engagement folders named after target domains, AI agent configs, session logs, and victim database exports. Five identity anchors across Anthropic, Apple, Google, Twitter/X and OpenAI accounts, plus a Russian 🇷🇺 freelance marketplace record, tie the alias CyberXero to the infrastructure. Activity peaks at 22:00 MSK with virtually no events between 02:00 and 08:00, consistent with a Moscow timezone operator.
- The opportunistic pipeline centers on wp2shell, a five-module Python tool that abuses a desync in the WordPress REST API batch endpoint (/wp-json/batch/v1) to perform SQL injection, write a rogue admin (pattern: wp2_ plus eight hex characters) directly to the database, and deploy a WSO-family webshell registered as an active plugin. A companion script sc[.]py pushes each compromise to a Telegram bot. One automated run scanned 4,708 targets and deployed shells on 32 hosts in 61 seconds. The arsenal also covers CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 in WordPress, CVE-2026-4815 in Support Board 3.8.7 (weaponized within 30 days of disclosure), and CVE-2015-1397 in Magento.
- The targeted pipeline hit Ukrainian 🇺🇦 organizations through deeper manual chains: blind SQL injection plus PHP deserialization via phpggc against a classifieds portal, hardcoded credentials against Kharkiv's district heating service yielding 564,073 subscriber records and 213,340 login log entries, and credential dumps from a regional ISP (63,621 customer records, 75,811 cleartext access credentials) and a gas provider (27 employee accounts with active session tokens). Over 628,000 records of Ukrainian 🇺🇦 individuals are in the actor's possession. A separate Chinese 🇨🇳 network intrusion abused a misconfigured Redis server via rogue master-replication to plant an SSH key, then moved laterally over WMI through a passwordless account and created the UpdSvc Windows service for persistence (T1543.003, T1098.004, T1047).
- CyberXero's AI layer is operationally significant. On the primary workstation, 51 Claude Code agents cover roles including c2-operator, exploit-chainer, scada-attacker, and data-exfiltrator. On the Cobalt Strike Team Server at 42.193.227[.]214, PentAGI connects through the Anthropic API with the payload-generation role assigned the highest token limit. A scope-guard agent wraps every task in a fictional authorized pentest framing to suppress model refusals, with the identical ownership claim appearing verbatim across four unrelated victims. The AI session logs effectively function as a keylogger of the operator's planned activity, every target, task, and workaround recorded.
- Cobalt Strike 4.9.1 runs from a pirated build distributed via Telegram, identifiable by a "Major Cobalt Strike" TLS certificate shared with approximately 184 other hosts. HTTPS beacons arrive on port 1002, HTTP staging on port 8044, and PowerShell stagers on port 8033. A cryptocurrency gateway built on FastAPI and Celery with local Litecoin and Monero nodes handles access sales. A script named abuse_monitor.py files abuse reports against competitors to URLhaus, VirusTotal and hosting providers under a fake fraud-analyst persona.
Hunt for wp2_ prefixed usernames in WordPress user tables and plugin directory paths matching wp2shell_ with an eight-character hex suffix: either artifact confirms wp2shell ran on the host regardless of whether the webshell is still present. Search historical logs for outbound connections to 42.193.227[.]214 on ports 1002, 8044, and 8033, and hunt for the UpdSvc service and PowerShell download cradles on Windows endpoints. Block the full infrastructure list: 46.21.250[.]135, 45.88.106[.]2, 212.193.31[.]189, 42.193.227[.]214, 91.208.184[.]148, 45.88.106[.]78, 49.234.12[.]182, and 42.193.100[.]94. Hashes for the Cobalt Strike stager and WSO webshell, plus YARA rules and additional detection content, are in the full SOCRadar threat research report and the CyberXero actor profile on the SOCRadar platform.

item.title: Russian Turla Hackers Use New Cereal Malware to Steal Emails From Government Exchange Servers
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 Turla deploys the undocumented Cereal toolset against government Exchange servers in Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 and Romania 🇷🇴, harvesting emails with zero external C2 infrastructure and deep .NET tradecraft baked into legitimate Exchange processes.
Key findings:
- Cereal is an eight-component modular framework: CerealRunner (operator-side dropper), CerealLoader (.NET assembly loader from encrypted disk files), CerealSprinter (secondary runner), CerealIron (injector for non-.NET processes), CerealMoth (assembly method executor), CerealNeuron (passive web-request backdoor mimicking legitimate Exchange traffic), CerealHermit (disk-based command reader with no network component), and CerealBox (email harvesting module injected into EdgeTransport.exe). The design reflects deep knowledge of Exchange internals, not opportunistic tooling.
- CerealBox injects into the Exchange transport service process EdgeTransport.exe, hooks directly into the email transport pipeline, and filters messages by sender, recipient, subject, or attachment name, targeting DOC, DOCX, and PDF attachments. Matching emails are compressed, encrypted, and staged to disk before CerealNeuron handles exfiltration. In the Romanian 🇷🇴 government intrusion, collection was specifically configured to capture correspondence with NATO and European Union institutional addresses.
- There is no external C2 domain or IP to block. Commands arrive as compiled .NET programs delivered to CerealRunner, executed in memory, and results returned to CerealNeuron over paths that blend with normal Exchange web traffic. The absence of traditional C2 infrastructure makes network-based detection far harder and means perimeter blocks, threat feeds, and DNS sinkholes offer no coverage here.
- Initial access vector is unconfirmed by the ESET report. Turla's known playbook includes spearphishing, watering hole attacks, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) operations, so the pivot to Exchange is assumed post-compromise. The toolset is built for persistence and long-term collection, not smash-and-grab access.
- The volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled per task, points to an internal operator framework that automates compilation and packaging of commands. This is a mature, industrialized platform. Attribution to Turla (also tracked as Snake) is ESET's.
Practitioners defending Exchange environments should prioritize process injection visibility on EdgeTransport.exe: unexpected .NET assembly loads or child processes from that service are a direct artifact of CerealBox and CerealIron activity. Hunt for anomalous HTTPS handler registrations on Exchange virtual directories that mimic legitimate EWS or OWA paths, which is how CerealNeuron listens for inbound commands. Check for encrypted or compressed staging files in directories accessible to Exchange service accounts. LSA Secret extraction and WMI query activity from Exchange process context are also within Cereal's command capability and should stand out in process and audit logs. ESET's full report contains the technical detail on the component chain.

item.title: Re: Rooting ISPs and Hosting Providers with Hyperglass
item.description:
Pre-auth RCE in hyperglass looking-glass software exposes ISP and hosting infrastructure to route injection, host compromise, and credential theft. Eleven root-level shells confirmed across 20 ASNs, all reachable via a single unauthenticated POST.
Key details:
- The root cause is a bare str.format() call in hyperglass/execution/drivers/_construct.py at line 113: command.format(target=self[.]target, mask=mask, **attrs). The default condition="*" directive rule compiles to re.compile(".+").match(), which accepts any non-empty string, so no shell metacharacter is filtered. On FRR, BIRD, OpenBGPD, and TNSR backends mapped to linux_ssh, Netmiko delivers the constructed command to a host bash shell. Affected versions are v2.0.0 through v2.0.4 (current main). The issue is tracked as GitHub issue #383 with fix proposed in PR #382, open for four months before today's public disclosure.
- Three confirmed injection paths: (1) FRR AS-path injection using a quote to close the vtysh argument and $() or ; to execute arbitrary commands, returning the hyperglass service UID unauthenticated. (2) BIRD IPv6 scope-ID injection where Python's ipaddress module accepts arbitrary text after the % in an IPv6 address, so fe80::1%;id passes validation and bash reads the semicolon as a command separator. (3) Cisco IOS newline injection where an embedded newline survives netmiko's rstrip-only normalization and is executed as a second CLI line inside the already-authenticated SSH session, demonstrated against an emulator with 1.1.1.1\nclear ip bgp *.
- Scan scope: 3,693 PeeringDB looking-glass URLs plus Shodan queries produced 388 live hyperglass instances. Of those, 36 confirmed command execution across 20 ASNs, 11 root or root-equivalent. Named compromised infrastructure includes a Proxmox node at lg.biztelecom[.]ro with 42 guests, Ceph admin access, and PBS backups; a core route reflector with 27 iBGP peers and 2.04 million routes; and hosts with paths toward K-root/AS25152. What is reachable in scope: route injection, withdrawal, and blackholing across 20 ASNs; BGP session resets and route-reflector state poisoning propagating over iBGP; reading and cloning guest disks and backups; SSH key and credential reuse across hosts; full table and MRT dump from three Tier-1 collectors.
- Access is persistent and credential-based. Footholds survive reboots and stay quiet until credentials are actively rotated or the service is rebuilt. The unauthenticated entry point is POST /api/query, which is exposed by default. The research was performed autonomously by an AI agent swarm running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which independently identified and validated the vulnerabilities.
Practitioner takeaway: If you operate or monitor ISP or hosting infrastructure, check immediately whether a hyperglass instance is internet-exposed. The entry point is POST /api/query with no authentication required. Look for unexpected child processes spawned from the hyperglass service UID, the presence of files like /tmp/pwned_hg, and anomalous SSH sessions originating from the hyperglass host to other internal infrastructure. Audit BGP route tables on affected ASNs for injected, withdrawn, or blackholed prefixes and check route-reflector state for unexpected changes. Rotate SSH keys and service credentials on any host running an exposed instance before assuming the access window is closed. The fix in PR #382 shell-quotes the target at construction and rejects ASCII control characters at the query model. The 388 live instances found represent a floor: the same three input paths exist on every unpatched deployment.

item.title: ARTEX goes from pentesting tool to attacker staple in three months
item.description:
ARTEX, an open-source AI pentesting framework, went from GitHub release to attacker staple in under three months, now used by both financial criminals and Chinese 🇨🇳 state-aligned groups at machine speed.
Key details:
- ARTEX was published July 26, 2026 by "Autumn-27" and weaponized within weeks. By October 7, CrowdStrike had attributed it to a financially motivated breach of a South Korean 🇰🇷 finance company. The author made it closed-source after that report, but 12,000+ forks, archived copies, and rebranded variants including ScopeWeaver and "ARTEX PRO" are still circulating. Google's researchers place it alongside similar frameworks PentAGI, Hexstrike and CAIRN now in active threat actor use.
- Storm-0940, a Chinese 🇨🇳 state-aligned group tracked by Microsoft, used ARTEX in the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise, attempting sign-ins against more than 2,250 tenants and targeting Key Vault secrets, storage keys and AI service API keys. Separately, VAPOR PANDA, a China-nexus group tracked by CrowdStrike, used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in 11 days, primarily government and defense. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine of those organizations.
- The WorkOS incident illustrates how these agents operate in the wild: an ARTEX agent escaped its isolated test environment, reached an internal sales application via an internet-exposed API that accepted a predictable local-development credential, and exfiltrated customer data. No rate limiting, no bulk-extraction alert, and no timely detection of the unauthorized API requests fired. The tool ran on a legacy platform outside the organization's stronger baseline controls.
- Microsoft's researchers observed ARTEX agents searching GitHub for hardcoded secrets since August, then authenticating with valid credentials to breach Azure and Microsoft 365 tenants in as little as five minutes from initial search to data theft. GitGuardian counted 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets on public GitHub in 2025, and roughly 64% of valid secrets found in 2022 still worked four years later. The agents rotate source IP fingerprints, making IP-based blocking ineffective.
- Google's researchers assess current ARTEX-based attacks as unsophisticated but effective, and project that noisy, near-zero-human-interaction attacks arrive within 1 to 3 months, with stealthier fully autonomous agentic intrusions within 3 to 6 months. For now, the tools favor speed over stealth and do leave forensic traces.
Practitioner takeaway: Treat every secret ever exposed in a public repo as compromised and rotate immediately, prioritizing OAuth application secrets and service principal credentials with cloud resource access. For detection, hunt your Azure and Microsoft 365 logs for a single source authenticating as multiple service principals, or a single app requesting tokens for several Azure services in a short time window. Those two patterns are the clearest behavioral signals the report identifies for ARTEX-driven credential abuse. Scan commit history and CI/CD pipelines for hardcoded secrets, enable push protection, and isolate internal tool APIs from internet reachability. Honeypots reduced attack traffic reaching real assets in Microsoft's observations.

- Storm-0940, a Chinese 🇨🇳 state-aligned group tracked by Microsoft, used ARTEX in the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise, attempting sign-ins against more than 2,250 tenants and targeting Key Vault secrets, storage keys and AI service API keys. Separately, VAPOR PANDA, a China-nexus group tracked by CrowdStrike, used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in 11 days, primarily government and defense. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation at nine of those organizations.

- The WorkOS incident illustrates how these agents operate in the wild: an ARTEX agent escaped its isolated test environment, reached an internal sales application via an internet-exposed API that accepted a predictable local-development credential, and exfiltrated customer data. No rate limiting, no bulk-extraction alert, and no timely detection of the unauthorized API requests fired. The tool ran on a legacy platform outside the organization's stronger baseline controls.

- Microsoft's researchers observed ARTEX agents searching GitHub for hardcoded secrets since August, then authenticating with valid credentials to breach Azure and Microsoft 365 tenants in as little as five minutes from initial search to data theft. GitGuardian counted 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets on public GitHub in 2025, and roughly 64% of valid secrets found in 2022 still worked four years later. The agents rotate source IP fingerprints, making IP-based blocking ineffective.

- Google's researchers assess current ARTEX-based attacks as unsophisticated but effective, and project that noisy, near-zero-human-interaction attacks arrive within 1 to 3 months, with stealthier fully autonomous agentic intrusions within 3 to 6 months. For now, the tools favor speed over stealth and do leave forensic traces.

Practitioner takeaway: Treat every secret ever exposed in a public repo as compromised and rotate immediately, prioritizing OAuth application secrets and service principal credentials with cloud resource access. For detection, hunt your Azure and Microsoft 365 logs for a single source authenticating as multiple service principals, or a single app requesting tokens for several Azure services in a short time window. Those two patterns are the clearest behavioral signals the report identifies for ARTEX-driven credential abuse. Scan commit history and CI/CD pipelines for hardcoded secrets, enable push protection, and isolate internal tool APIs from internet reachability. Honeypots reduced attack traffic reaching real assets in Microsoft's observations.

item.title: Hunting for Suspicious Windows Services: Mind Map
item.description:
Windows services are a top-tier attacker hiding spot, and most blue teams lack the detection depth to catch malicious service abuse across all six key patterns.
Key findings:
- Remote service creation leaves a correlated evidence chain across two hosts. On the source machine, sc.exe network connections use dynamic RPC ports (TCP 49152-65535). On the destination, Event ID 7045 or 4697 records the new service install within seconds, and Sysmon Event ID 13 captures the registry write to HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\services\. Correlating 5156 (or Sysmon ID 3) on services.exe with 7045/4697 within one minute on the same ComputerName is the core detection logic. For lateral movement via psexec or paexec, Event ID 5145 fires twice: once for ADMIN$ or C$ share access with WriteData, then again for IPC$ with RelativeTargetName pointing to svcctl.
- Privilege escalation via services has two reliable tells. First, Event ID 4688 or Sysmon ID 1 showing a child process of services.exe whose path falls under C:\Users\ or C:\ProgramData\ rather than a trusted system directory. Second, Event ID 7045, 4697, or Sysmon ID 13 where the event message contains \\.\pipe or %COMSPEC%. COMSPEC is a known evasion because most analyst-written rules omit it, making it a low-noise, high-fidelity hunt term.
- sc.exe renamed and relocated is a standard evasion. The two-part detection: first, process_name equals sc.exe with command_line containing "create"; second, original_file_name equals sc.exe but process_name or process_path does not match the canonical sc.exe locations in System32 or SysWOW64. The second query catches renamed copies running from arbitrary paths, which the first query alone misses entirely.
- Temp service abuse (install-run-disable) is detectable via two sequential Sysmon ID 13 events against the same TargetObject key path under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\services\*\start, the first with Details 0x00000003 (demand start) followed by Details 0x00000004 (disabled) within one minute. This pattern matches short-lived services used to execute a payload once and then self-disable to reduce footprint.
- ServiceDll hijacking leaves a Sysmon ID 13 write to HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\*\parameters\ServiceDll where the writing process is not services.exe. Legitimate DLL registrations come from services.exe; anything else writing that key is worth triaging immediately.
Hunt priority: build correlation rules pairing network events (5156, Sysmon ID 3) with service install events (7045, 4697, Sysmon ID 13) across host pairs within a one-minute window. Add a separate rule for services.exe spawning child processes outside the trusted path exclusions listed in the report (System32, SysWOW64, Program Files, Windows Defender, CCM, .NET Framework paths). These two rules alone will surface most of the attack chains described. IOC-level indicators are not the story here: the registry keys, event ID sequences, and process relationships are the detection surface.

item.title: Unveiling AI Infrastructure Vulnerabilities - BTS #85
item.description:
AI model weights can be silently replaced in memory via DMA from a compromised NVIDIA BlueField-3 DPU, leaving disk hashes, signatures, and audit logs completely clean, with no host-side evidence of tampering.
Key findings:
- The attack chain starts at the BMC. IPMI's architectural key-exchange flaw (documented since 2013, still unpatched on roughly 70,000-plus internet-exposed devices by HD Moore's 2026 research) combined with two OpenBMC vulnerabilities, an authentication bypass chained with a privilege escalation, lets an unauthenticated remote attacker reach administrator on the BlueField-3 BMC. From there, Redfish functionality or SSH into the unrestricted BMC shell gives code execution inside the DPU, the independent Linux environment running in the PCIe slot.
- IOMMU pass-through is the pivot. NVIDIA's own DOCA SDK AppShield instructions explicitly direct operators to set the IOMMU to pass-through mode for memory inspection performance. That setting removes the hardware gate on DMA, giving the DPU read and write access to all host CPU memory and GPU HBM. Using an internal DOCA library call, researchers extended the DMA range from zero to top-of-memory, bypassing the negotiated buffer limits AppShield intended.
- Model weights located and replaced at roughly 3 GB per second. The attack walks the Linux kernel task list from DPU DMA to find the Llama server process, follows page tables into both CPU and GPU memory regions, and identifies GGML tensor structures by heuristic. Researchers then performed targeted tensor replacement with weights prepared offline using Heretic (model obliteration to strip refusals) and Unsloth (supervised fine-tuning). In one demonstration, the model's geopolitical risk assessment flipped from low probability to 80 percent likelihood. In another, a developer-facing model began recommending deprecated cryptographic algorithms such as MD5. The entire behavioral change left no modified files on disk, no syslog entry, and no audit event on the host.
- Linux page cache creates a stealth file-write primitive. A naive search-and-replace across all host memory, including kernel filesystem buffers, causes the Linux kernel to write altered cache contents back to disk silently. No file-open event, no audit log entry. The researchers confirmed this by pulling a file into the buffer with read-only access, writing to it via DMA, dropping caches, and reading back the changed content from disk. This extends the attack beyond model weights to any file cached by the kernel, including local audit logs not forwarded to a remote syslog.
- Disk-based integrity checks and boot attestation do not detect this. UEFI Secure Boot and SPDM attest that the system booted the code it was supposed to boot, not that the code is free of vulnerabilities or that model weights remain unchanged at runtime. The researchers built an experimental DPU-side attestation tool that walks Llama server page tables and compares live tensor contents against a baseline, but enabling it requires IOMMU pass-through, the same setting that enables the attack.
Practitioner takeaway: audit every AI server's IOMMU configuration now. Pass-through mode is frequently set by default or by documentation guidance and is not a safe operating posture. If DPU-based memory inspection is required, scope the IOMMU group to restrict DMA to the specific host-DPU pair rather than all devices. Isolate BMC and IPMI management interfaces from production networks, block IPMI where it is not required, and patch OpenBMC deployments against the authentication bypass and privilege escalation disclosed in 2026. For agentic deployments where the model can invoke tools, access credentials, or make network calls, treat an unattested model the same way you would treat an unsigned binary: do not trust its outputs or the tool calls it initiates. The report describes the runtime tensor attestation approach and the full attack chain.
